newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court hears judge's sex assault case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court hears judge's sex assault case.

text.p: A Justice Department lawyer urged the Supreme Court Tuesday to uphold the conviction under a federal civil rights law of a former Tennessee state judge for sexually assaulting five women in his chambers.

"The defendant was properly and constitutionally convicted in this case," Deputy Solicitor General Seth Waxman said, arguing the law does apply to sexual assaults by public officials in the course of their duties.
He said the judge, David Lanier, 62, who came from a politically powerful family, acted wilfully and that the women had a constitutional right to be free from unwanted sexual abuse.

The 1874 law at issue was adopted after the Civil War to protect the civil rights of blacks. It most often has been used by federal prosecutors to protect against local government brutality by police or other officials.
The law does not expressly make a crime of sexual assaults committed against court employees or litigants by a state judge, a federal appeals court said in overturning the judge's conviction.

Chief Justice William Rehnquist asked if some of the sexual assault incidents involved less serious misdemeanor charges. Waxman acknowledged they did, but said the most serious charge concerned a woman forced to have oral sex with Lanier.
"There is a real element of vagueness in all this," Rehnquist complained after Waxman said the standard involved showing "a serious and substantial intrusion."
Justice Antonin Scalia expressed concern about applying the law too broadly, saying it was not designed to cover "a state official who punches someone" or other physical assaults.

But Waxman rejected such concerns, saying in response to a question from Justice Anthony Kennedy that the law could not be applied to a janitor who jumps from a closet in the Supreme Court and rapes a woman.
Lanier, a former Tennessee Chancery Court judge, was convicted on seven counts of wilfully depriving a person of rights protected under the Constitution.

The convictions stemmed from sexual assaults in 1989 to 1991. The victims were in his chambers in connection with their official court jobs or prospective employment, including one woman who had a child custody case before Lanier.
Lanier committed one of the assaults while wearing his judicial robe, according to court records.
Lanier's attorney Alfred Knight argued the government's position means "any assault by any public employee could be covered" by the law.
Justice Stephen Breyer what the difference was between being free from offensive sexual conduct and the protections a citizen has not to be beat up by a policeman.

Knight admitted sexual abuse was part of the "continuum" on the use of excessive force. He noted the same law had been used in the conviction of two Los Angeles police officers in the beating of black motorist Rodney King.
After the hour-long arguments, the justices took the case under advisement, with a ruling expected by June.
